1

  • N: šiduri | sābītu || ša ina sapan (|) tâmti | ašbat
  • T: Šiduri was an ale-wife who lived by the sea-shore.
  • L: šiduri ← Šiduri I; sābītu ← sābītu I “female brewer, alehouse keeper O/jB”; ša ← ša I “who(m), which”; ina ← ina I “(im-m..., ip-p... etc.) in, on”; sapan ← sapannu I “flatland, plain Bab., NA between mountains”; tâmti ← tiāmtu I “jB pl. also timiāti sea”; ašbat ← ašābu I “to sit (down)”
NinNAQuo1 vi 21. {munus}si-d[u-ri sa-bi-t]u₄ ša₂ ina sa#-pan tam-ti aš₂-bat
NinNA1c i 1. {d}ši₂-du-ri sa-bi-t[u₄ & ša₂ ina sa-pan tam-ti aš₂-bat]
BabNB1 i 1. [x x x x x x x x x x x t]am-ti₃ aš₂-b[a-tu₄]

2

  • N: ašbat | [ ... ] ... [ ... ]
  • T: there she lived, [in an inn by the sea-shore.]
  • L: ašbat ← ašābu I “to sit (down)”
NinNA1c i 2. aš₂-bat-ma & [x x x x (x)]
BabNB1 i 2. [x x x x x x] x [x]

3

  • N: ibšûši | kannū || ibšûši | ... [ ... ]
  • T: Potstands she had, and [vats of gold,]
  • L: ibšûši ← bašû I “to be (at hand, available)”; kannū ← kannu I “(vessel-)stand”; ibšûši ← bašû I “to be (at hand, available)”
  • Note: See [RN117: 868]: “It is conventional to restore the end of this line after the Hittite version, which states that Siduri had [na]m-z[i]-tum ša KU.SI[G₁₇], ‘a vat of gold’ (KUB XVII 3 iii 9,ed. Friedrich, ZA 39, p.22; cf. Parpola, SAA Gilg.).The sign nam is compatible with the traces, and kannu and namzītu are the two principal fittings of a brewery, well attested in numerous texts (see CAD K, p. 155). However, such a restoration raises a problem of agreement with the verb. Some interpret this as ep-šu-ši, i.e. plural stative of epēšu; I have followed a suggestion of A. Westenholz in taking the word from the more neutral bašû. However that may be, epšūand ibšû are both masculine and namzītu is feminine, so that for the moment it does not seem safe to restore either n[am-zi-tu or n[am-za-tu (pl.).
NinNA1c i 3. ib-šu-ši kan-nu ib-šu-ši x [x x x]

4

  • N: kutummi | kuttumat-ma || k[ulūli | kullulat?]
  • T: she was swathed in hoods and [veiled with] veils.
  • L: kutummi ← kutummu I “cover(ing) Bab., OA”; kuttumat-ma ← kuttumu I “covered over j/NB”; k[ulūli ← kulūlu I “crown M/NA, j/NB as mark of royalty”; kullulat?] ← kullulu II
  • Note: The restoration follows the suggestion in [RN117: 869].
NinNA1c i 4. ku-tu-um-mi kut-tu-mat-ma & k[u?-lu?-li? x x x (x)]

5

  • N: gilgāmeš | uttaggiša[m]-ma | ... [ ... ]
  • T: Gilgameš came wandering, and […:]
  • L: gilgāmeš ← Gilgameš I; uttaggiša[m]-ma ← nagāšu I “to go to(wards) O/jB”
  • Parallels: cf. L I.4 OB "VA+BM" a+12
NinNA1c i 5. {d}GIŠ-gim₂-maš ut-tag-gi-ša[m]-ma & x [x x (x)]

6

  • N: maška | labiš || pul[u]ht[a | ... ]
  • T: he was clothed in a pelt, and fearful [to look on.]
  • L: maška ← mašku I “skin of human”; labiš ← labāšu I “to clothe o.s.”; pul[u]ht[a ← puluhtu I “fear(someness) Bab., NA”
  • Note: The restorations naši, mali, and īšu for the last word are suggested in [RN117: 869], who adds: “The recovery of the penultimate word allows one to see that the phrase anticipates the action to come. The lion’s skin makes Gilgameš frightening to behold, and in due course Šiduri is terrified at the sight of him.”
NinNA1c i 6. maš-ka la-biš & pu-l[uh?-tu₄? x (x) x]
BabNB1 i 6. [x x x x pu-lu]h?-t[u₄ x (x) x]

7

  • N: īši | šīr (|) il[ī] | ina z[umrīšu?]
  • T: He had the flesh of the gods in [his body,]
  • L: īši ← išû I “to have (no pres., pret. īši, īšu”; šīr ← šīru I “often pl. flesh”; il[ī] ← ilu I “pl. ilū, ilānu god, deity a or the god, also du.”; ina ← ina I “(im-m..., ip-p... etc.) in, on”; z[umrīšu?] ← zumru I “body”
  • Parallels: cf. L I.4 SB "IX" 49
NinNA1c i 7. i-ši UZU DINGIR-M[E]Š & ina z[u-um-ri-šu?]
BabNB1 i 7. [x x x x DINGIR-ME]Š i[na x x x x x]

  • L: ibašši ← bašû I “to be (at hand, available)”; nissatu ← nissatu I “wailing, lamentation O/jB, NA”; ina ← ina I “(im-m..., ip-p... etc.) in, on”; [karš]ī[šu] ← karšu I “m. & f. stomach, interior”

318

  • N: lullâ | mītu || ul ikruba | ina māti
  • N (variant, other manuscripts): lullû | amēlu | edil | ultu ikrubū | [ ... ]
  • T: The dead do not greet man in the land.
  • L: lullâ ← lullû I “primeval man O/jB created by gods”; mītu ← mītu I “dead transf. of the (politically) powerless, of city or country”; ul ← ul I “not Bab., to negate main clause”; ikruba ← karābu II “to pray, bless, greet”; ina ← ina I “(im-m..., ip-p... etc.) in, on”; māti ← mātu I “f. land, country”
  • Note: As noted by [RN117: 877], the line probably means “that the dead, once their shades are successfully delivered to the Netherworld, have no further contact with the living. The preterite verb can be explained as ‘gnomic’, indicative of a proverbial saying.” The reading here follows the suggestion in [george2010assyrian: 212 fn. 24], according to which karābu would be an ancient gloss that provides the infinitive of ikruba, rather than a paranomastic infinitive.
  • Note: The variant line reads: “Mortal man is imprisoned. After they blessed [me,].” See the discussion on the two versions of this line in [RN117: 876–877], who considers the variant from Nineveh inferior (on the idea that the “dead man” is a “prisoner,” see [chiodi1995prigioniero: 159–171]).
